title: Defensive design: input validation and authentication
specPoints: 2.3.1 **Defensive design** considerations: anticipating misuse, **authentication**, **input validation** (range, type, length, presence, format checks) and **input sanitisation**
Write code that validates input and authenticates users
learn: Explain what defensive design is and why programs must expect bad input and misuse
Name the five validation checks (range, type, length, presence, format) and give an example of each
Write validation loops that reject bad input and explain the problem to the user
Explain authentication (username/password, limits on attempts) and write a simple version
Distinguish validation (is it acceptable?) from sanitisation (removing dangerous content) and from verification (did you mean it?)
hook: Type your age as 'twelve'. Type −5. Type 999. Leave it blank. Paste in a whole paragraph. A program written for the user who always types the right thing lasts about a day in a real school. Defensive design is writing for the user who doesn't.

video.title: Expect the worst: validation and authentication
video.brief: 4 minutes. A form field with a stream of bad inputs bouncing off five labelled shields: range, type, length, presence, format. Each shield lights as it catches its input. Then a login box: password checked against stored value, attempts counter, lockout after 3. Close with the three words on screen: validation (is it allowed?), verification (is it what you meant?), sanitisation (strip the dangerous bits).

p: **Defensive design** means writing a program on the assumption that users will make mistakes, misuse it, or attack it — and making sure it keeps working anyway. Three parts in the spec: **anticipating misuse** (what could go wrong at each input?), **authentication** (is this person allowed?) and **input validation** (is this data acceptable?).

explain.code:
Check      Question it asks                       Example
Range      Is it between the allowed limits?      age between 0 and 120; mark 0–100
Type       Is it the right kind of data?          a whole number, not "twelve" or 3.5
Length     Is it the right number of characters?  password at least 8; postcode at most 8
Presence   Has something been entered at all?     name is not blank
Format     Does it match the expected pattern?    email contains @ and .; date is DD/MM/YYYY
after: In the exam, name the check **and** say what it checks for in this scenario. 'Range check' alone is half a mark; 'range check to make sure the mark is between 0 and 100' is the full mark.

p: The pattern is always: ask, test, loop while bad. Tell the user *why* it was rejected. Python's `try/except` handles the type check without crashing:
explain.code:
def get_mark():
    while True:
        text = input("Mark (0-100): ")
        if text == "":                       # presence
            print("Please enter a mark.")
        elif not text.isdigit():             # type (whole number)
            print("Numbers only.")
        elif int(text) < 0 or int(text) > 100:   # range
            print("Must be 0 to 100.")
        else:
            return int(text)

# OCR pseudocode style
do
    mark = int(input("Mark (0-100): "))
    if mark < 0 OR mark > 100 then
        print("Must be 0 to 100")
    endif
until mark >= 0 AND mark <= 100

p: **Authentication** checks that the user is who they claim to be, usually a username and password compared against stored values. Defensive extras the exam likes: a limit on failed attempts (then lock out or delay), minimum password length/complexity, not revealing *which* of username or password was wrong, and never storing passwords as plain text (hash them — detail is beyond GCSE, but say 'stored securely').
explain.code:
attempts = 0
while attempts < 3:
    user = input("Username: ")
    pwd = input("Password: ")
    if user == stored_user and pwd == stored_pwd:
        print("Welcome")
        break
    attempts = attempts + 1
    print("Incorrect. Attempts left:", 3 - attempts)
if attempts == 3:
    print("Account locked")

list: **Validation**: is the input *allowed*? (A date of birth in 2090 is not.)
**Verification**: is the input *what the user meant*? (Type your email twice; 'Are you sure?')

**Sanitisation**: *removing or escaping dangerous content* from input before using it — e.g. stripping characters that could form an SQL command (1.4 SQL injection) or script tags. Valid input can still be dangerous; sanitisation handles that.

p: People type the wrong thing. Good programs check every input and say what is wrong instead of crashing.
Ask. Test. If bad, say why and ask again.
simple.code:
mark = int(input("Mark 0-100: "))
while mark < 0 or mark > 100:
    print("Must be 0 to 100.")
    mark = int(input("Mark 0-100: "))

p: **Authentication** = username and password. Count the attempts. After 3 wrong, lock them out.

keyterms.def: Designing a program so it keeps working when users make mistakes or try to misuse it.
Checking that input is acceptable before using it: range, type, length, presence, format.
Checking that a user is who they claim to be, e.g. with a username and password.
Removing or neutralising potentially dangerous content from input.
Checking that input is what the user intended, e.g. entering it twice.
Thinking ahead about how a program could be used wrongly and guarding against it.

try.title: 1. Break it, then defend it
p: Run it and type: `twelve`, `-5`, `999`, nothing at all. Note what happens each time. Then rewrite it using the `get_mark()` pattern from the lesson so none of those break it.

try.title: 2. Five checks, five functions
p: Write a validated input function for each: `get_age()` (range 0–120, type), `get_name()` (presence, length 2–30), `get_email()` (format: contains @ and a dot after it), `get_postcode()` (length ≤ 8, presence), `get_yes_no()` (format: y or n). Each must loop until valid and say what was wrong.

try.title: 3. Login with lockout
p: Finish the login: three attempts, a message with attempts remaining, lockout after the third failure, and the same message whether the username or the password was wrong. Then add a minimum password length check when the account is created.

try.title: 4. Sanitise
p: A comment box will be shown on a web page. Write `sanitise(text)` that removes `<` and `>` and any `;` or `--`, and trims spaces at both ends. Test it with `<script>alert(1)</script>` and with `Robert'); DROP TABLE Students;--`.
try.code:
def sanitise(text):
    pass

print(sanitise("<script>alert(1)</script>"))
print(sanitise("  Robert'); DROP TABLE Students;--  "))

try.title: 5. Validation in blocks
instructions: Build the mark validation loop in Python Blocks and compare the generated code with your Try 1 solution.

check.q: Checking that a mark is between 0 and 100 is a:
Checking that a field has not been left blank is a:
Asking the user to type a new password twice is:
check.fb: Checks they meant what they typed.

check.q: Removing `<script>` tags from a comment before storing it is:
A sensible defensive feature for a login is:
opts: Telling the user which part was wrong
Locking the account after several failed attempts
Storing passwords in a text file

exam.q: A program asks the user to enter their date of birth as a day, month and year. Describe **two** validation checks that could be performed on the month, and give an example of invalid data each would reject.
model: Range check: month must be between 1 and 12 (1), rejecting e.g. 13 (1). Type check: month must be a whole number (1), rejecting e.g. "March" or 3.5 (1).
exam.commentary: Name the check, state the rule for *this* field, give an example that fails it. Presence check is also acceptable. Two different checks — two range checks score once.

exam.q: Write pseudocode that asks a user for a password and repeats until the password entered is at least 8 characters long.
model: Input stored in a variable (1). Loop controlled by the length — `while password.length < 8` / `do…until password.length >= 8` (1). Message and repeated input inside the loop (1).
exam.commentary: Length check in a loop. `len(password)` in Python. The repeat-input-inside-the-loop mark is the one students drop.

exam.q: Explain **two** ways a login system could be made more secure through defensive design.
model: Limit the number of failed attempts and lock the account / add a delay (1), which prevents brute-force guessing of passwords (1). Require a minimum password length / mix of characters (1), which makes passwords harder to guess or crack (1). Also acceptable: not revealing whether the username or password was wrong; storing passwords securely (hashed).
exam.commentary: Each way needs a reason — 'what' plus 'why it helps'. Two features without reasons: two marks.

home: Take the calculator or quiz program you wrote earlier in 2.2 and add validation to every input, with a clear message for each kind of bad input. Write a list of the checks you added and which of the five types each one is.

teacher.timing: 60 min: hook 4 · explain 12 · try 28 · check 5 · exam 8 · homework 3
misconceptions: Validation guarantees the input is *correct*. It guarantees it is *acceptable* — a plausible wrong age still passes.
'Type check' answered as 'check it's a number' when the field is text, and vice versa.
Authentication confused with validation; authentication is about the *person*.
say: 'Name the check. Say the rule. Give the bad example.'
'Valid is not the same as true. 25 is a valid age for anyone in this room — and wrong for all of you.'
teacher.skip: Try 4 (sanitise) and Try 5 are optional; Try 1–3 are the exam skills.
differentiation: Support: Try 2 — do `get_age()` together, then students complete two of the others.
Stretch: Try 3 — add a 10-second delay doubling after each failure (`time.sleep`) and explain the trade-off with usability.
